course: CMU 21-254: Linear Algebra and Vector Calculus for Engineers
audience: SI leader teaching live on a whiteboard. This is not a student worksheet.
toneRule: Keep explanations very simple, verbal, and board-friendly. Avoid textbook phrasing unless the problem needs it.
title: Exam 2 Review
sessionGoal: Students should review the core Exam 2 skills: inverses, determinants, eigenvalues/eigenvectors, diagonalization, projections, and cross product.
quickStartIfUnprepared: Start by saying: Exam 2 is mostly about what matrices do and what directions they preserve.
Do Problems 2 and 3 if eigenstuff is the priority.
Do Problems 4 and 5 if students want vector geometry review.
Use Problem 1 as a quick warm-up to connect inverses and determinants.
sayThisFirst: For Exam 2, always ask: is this an algebra question, an eigenvalue question, or a geometry question?
Invertibility is about whether a matrix can be undone.
Eigenvectors are directions that do not rotate under the matrix.
Diagonalization is useful because it makes powers easy.
Projection and cross product are geometry tools.
boardPlan: Finish with projection and cross product geometry.
keyFormulas: A matrix is diagonalizable when it has enough independent eigenvectors.
\(\|a\times b\|\) = area of the parallelogram spanned by \(a\) and \(b\).
commonMistakes: Assuming a repeated eigenvalue automatically means not diagonalizable.
Mixing up algebraic multiplicity and geometric multiplicity.
Putting eigenvectors as rows instead of columns in P.
Using cross product in 2D without first embedding or using the correct formula.
Forgetting that \(AB\) and \(BA\) may have different behavior.
notationWarnings: Use \(\lambda\) for eigenvalues and \(v\) for eigenvectors.
Use \(PDP^{-1}\) and keep the columns of P matched with the diagonal entries of D.
Use arrows like \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) for vectors between points.

problems.title: Inverse warm-up with a system
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: determinant first tells us whether the inverse exists.

drawInstructions: Write determinant nonzero means the map can be undone.

walkthrough.label: Check the determinant
walkthrough.latex: \[\det(A)=2(1)-1(1)=1.\] Since the determinant is not zero, \(A^{-1}\) exists.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the determinant in the denominator.
Switching the wrong entries in the inverse formula.
Solving \(bA^{-1}\) instead of \(A^{-1}b\).

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 4 for inverses and determinants.

problems.title: Repeated eigenvalue and diagonalizability
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \[A=\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\0&3\end{bmatrix}.\] Find the eigenvalue, find its eigenspace, and decide whether \(A\) is diagonalizable.
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: repeated eigenvalues are not automatically bad. The real question is how many independent eigenvectors we get.

drawInstructions: Draw one invariant direction along the x-axis.
Show that there is only one independent eigenvector direction.
Explain that a 2 by 2 matrix needs two independent eigenvectors to diagonalize.

walkthrough.label: Read the eigenvalue
walkthrough.latex: Since \(A\) is triangular, the eigenvalue is the diagonal entry: \[\lambda=3\] with algebraic multiplicity 2.

walkthrough.label: Find the eigenspace
walkthrough.latex: \[A-3I=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}.\] Solve \((A-3I)x=0\): \[x_2=0,\quad x_1\text{ is free}.\] So the eigenspace is \[\operatorname{span}\{(1,0)\}.\]

walkthrough.label: Decide diagonalizability
walkthrough.latex: The eigenspace is 1-dimensional, so there is only one independent eigenvector. A \(2\times2\) matrix needs two independent eigenvectors to be diagonalizable.

commonMistakes: Saying repeated eigenvalue means automatically not diagonalizable.
Forgetting to compute the eigenspace.
Thinking algebraic multiplicity and geometric multiplicity are always the same.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 5 for eigenvalues and eigenspaces.

problems.title: Use an eigenbasis to compute \(A^3x\)
problems.studentPromptLatex: Suppose \(v_1=(1,1)\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(4\), and \(v_2=(1,-1)\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(2\). If \(x=(3,1)\), compute \(A^3x\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: if a vector is written in the eigenbasis, powers of A just raise the eigenvalues to that power.

drawInstructions: Draw \(x\) as a combination of \(v_1\) and \(v_2\).
Under A^3, label the new vector as 2(4^3)v1+1(2^3)v2.

walkthrough.label: Apply A^3 to each eigenvector piece

commonMistakes: Multiplying the coordinates by \(4\) and \(2\) instead of \(4^3\) and \(2^3\).
Trying to compute \(A\) first even though the eigenbasis information is enough.
Forgetting to convert back to standard coordinates.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 6 for diagonalization and powers.

problems.title: Projection in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: the vector being projected onto controls the denominator.

drawInstructions: Draw u as the direction line.
Draw the perpendicular leftover from the projection tip to v.

walkthrough.label: Subtract to get the perpendicular part

commonMistakes: Using \(v\cdot v\) in the denominator.
Forgetting that \(v_{\perp}\) should be perpendicular to \(u\).
Mixing up \(\operatorname{proj}_{u}(v)\) and \(\operatorname{proj}_{v}(u)\).

problems.title: Cross product, normal vector, and area
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \(a=(1,2,0)\) and \(b=(3,-1,2)\). Compute \(a\times b\) and the area of the parallelogram spanned by \(a\) and \(b\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: cross product gives the normal vector, and its length gives the parallelogram area.

drawInstructions: Draw a and b starting at the same point.
Draw a normal vector labeled a x b.
Label the area as ||a x b||.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the negative sign on the \(\mathbf{j}\)-component.
Using dot product instead of cross product for area.
Reporting the cross product as the area instead of its magnitude.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 6 for cross product.

wrapUpQuestions: What is the difference between algebraic multiplicity and geometric multiplicity?
Why does diagonalization make powers easier?
When should you use projection vs. cross product?
qualityControlNotes: Exam review problems are original and cover the intended Exam 2 topics.
Checked projection and cross product arithmetic.
reviewSummary: Session 15 is an Exam 2 review set with five mixed problems and visual specs for each major geometry/eigen concept.

open.title: Exam 2: algebra, eigen, or geometry?
say: Welcome to Exam 2 review. Every problem on this exam falls into one of three families: undoing a matrix (inverses and determinants), eigen-questions, or geometry (projections and cross products).
Today, before we touch a problem, we'll name its family and its first move. That habit is worth more points than any single formula.

ask.q: Quick poll: which feels weakest right now: inverses and determinants, eigenvalues and diagonalization, or projections and cross products?
ask.a: Tally it on the board; linger on the most common answer.

write: undo a matrix → det ≠ 0? then the inverse
eigen → det(A − λI) = 0, then Nul(A − λI)
geometry → dot for along, cross for normal

idea.title: The Exam 2 map
say: Undoing: the determinant decides if an inverse exists; the inverse solves Ax = b in one multiplication.
Eigen: eigenvalues from det(A − λI) = 0, eigenvectors from the null space. Diagonalizable means enough independent eigenvectors, and that is what makes powers easy.
Geometry: the dot product splits a vector into along and across pieces; the cross product builds a normal whose length is an area.
draw: Draw three columns: 'Undo', 'Eigen', 'Geometry'. Under each, write its first move from the list.
As you finish each problem, write its one-line takeaway under its column.

ask.q: A problem says 'compute A¹⁰x'. Which family, and what's the first move?
ask.a: Eigen: write x as a combination of eigenvectors.

ask.q: A problem asks for the area of a triangle in 3D. First move?
ask.a: Geometry: take the cross product of two side vectors; the area is half its length.

launch.say: Warm-up from the 'Undo' column: find A⁻¹, then solve Ax = b.

askFirst.q: What do you check before any inverse?

steps.say: det A = 2 − 1 = 1. Nonzero: the inverse exists.

ask.q: What would det A = 0 have told you about Ax = b?
ask.a: No unique solution: either none or infinitely many.

steps.say: Swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by 1: [[1, −1], [−1, 2]].

ask.a: A times it: first row 2 − 1 = 1 and −2 + 2 = 0. ✓

steps.why: Always plug the answer back in. It takes ten seconds and catches sign slips.

si15-p1.meaning: A sends (3, 1) to (7, 4), and A⁻¹ undoes it. det A = 1 means A doesn't even change areas.

ifStuck.if: a student swaps the off-diagonal entries instead of the diagonal ones
ifStuck.then: multiply their answer by A; it won't give I.

si15-p1.transition: Next column: eigen. A repeated eigenvalue, and the question every exam asks about it.

launch.say: Find the eigenvalue, its eigenspace, and decide if A is diagonalizable.
circulate: Is anyone deciding from the repeated eigenvalue alone? Make them compute the eigenspace.

askFirst.q: Does a repeated eigenvalue automatically mean 'not diagonalizable'?
askFirst.a: No. It depends on whether the eigenspace is big enough.

ask.q: How many independent eigenvectors would we need?

steps.say: A − 3I = [[0, 1], [0, 0]] forces x₂ = 0. Only x₁ is free: E₃ = span{(1, 0)}.
One eigenvector direction, but we need two. Not diagonalizable.

ask.q: Which matrix with λ = 3 repeated IS diagonalizable?
ask.a: 3I itself: every vector is an eigenvector.

steps.why: This is a shear with a stretch: it tips every direction except the x-axis.

si15-p2.meaning: A stretches everything by 3 and also shears it sideways. Only the x-axis survives unturned, so there's no second eigenvector to build a basis.

ifStuck.if: a student claims (0, 1) is an eigenvector
ifStuck.then: compute A(0, 1) = (1, 3). Is that a multiple of (0, 1)?

si15-p2.transition: When there ARE enough eigenvectors, powers become easy. That's the next problem.

launch.say: Compute A³x using only the two eigenpairs. You never need A.

askFirst.a: Eigen/powers: write x as a combination of v₁ and v₂.

steps.say: (3, 1) = c₁(1, 1) + c₂(1, −1). Adding the equations: c₁ = 2, then c₂ = 1.
A³ acts on each piece separately: 2 · 4³ v₁ + 1 · 2³ v₂ = 128v₁ + 8v₂.

ask.q: Why can A³ act on each piece separately?

steps.why: In eigen-coordinates, A³ is just 'multiply coordinate 1 by 64 and coordinate 2 by 8'.

ask.q: Which eigenvector does A³x mostly point along?

si15-p3.meaning: Each application of A multiplies the (1, 1) part by 4 and the (1, −1) part by 2. The bigger eigenvalue wins, so Aⁿx swings toward (1, 1).

ifStuck.if: a student tries to find A
ifStuck.then: it's possible but slow; ask what A does to v₁ three times.

si15-p3.transition: On to the geometry column: a projection in 3D.

launch.say: Project v onto u and find the perpendicular part.
circulate: Ask finishers to check v⊥ · u = 0.

askFirst.q: Which vector's dot with itself goes in the denominator?
askFirst.a: u, the one we project onto.

ask.q: Is the angle between u and v acute?
Does it point the same way as u?

steps.why: The check is the whole reason this problem is easy to get right.

si15-p4.meaning: v splits into 5/3 of u plus a piece at a right angle to u. The length of that piece is v's distance from the line through u.

ifStuck.then: ask which direction the answer should point along.

si15-p4.transition: Last one: the cross product, and why its length is an area.

launch.say: Compute a × b and the area of the parallelogram they span.
circulate: The j-component has a minus in front.
Area is the length of a × b, not the vector.

askFirst.q: What two things does a × b tell you?
askFirst.a: Its direction is normal to a and b; its length is the parallelogram's area.

steps.say: Set up the determinant: i, j, k on top, then a, then b.

ask.q: Does the order of a and b matter?
ask.a: Yes: b × a = −(a × b). Same length, opposite direction.

ask.q: Area of the triangle with sides a and b?

steps.why: A zero cross product would mean a and b are parallel, so the parallelogram is flat.

si15-p5.meaning: (4, −2, −7) stands straight out of the plane containing a and b, and the parallelogram they span has area √69.

ifStuck.if: a student gets +2 in the middle
ifStuck.then: remind them of the + − + sign pattern across the top row.

wrap.write: Undo: det ≠ 0, then the inverse. Eigen: count independent eigenvectors; powers via eigen-coordinates. Geometry: dot for along/across, cross for normals and areas.

exit.a: AM: multiplicity as a root. GM: number of independent eigenvectors (dimension of the eigenspace).

exit.q: Why does diagonalization make powers easy?
exit.a: Aⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹, and Dⁿ just powers the diagonal.
Projection: how much of one vector lies along another. Cross: a vector perpendicular to both, with area as its length.

wrap.next: Good luck on Exam 2. After it: curves and functions of several variables.
